newsitem.title: UK: Britain admits radioactive waste dumping at sea.
newsitem.headline: Britain admits radioactive waste dumping at sea.

text.p: British fisheries ministry officials have discovered six probable examples of radioactive waste dumped at sea off the British Isles since World War Two which had previously been kept out of the public domain, a junior minister said on Wednesday.
The minister Jeff Rooker, said the amount of radiation involved should not be harmful to humans, but he had invited scientists to double check.

The government said on July 1 that low- to medium-level radioactive material, contained in metal drums encased in concrete, was disposed of during the 1950s in Beaufort's Dyke, a deep trench in the sea between Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Rooker said ministry investigations since then suggested a "damaged closed caesium-137 source" had been dumped in the same area in 1957 and 10,000 tonnes of building rubble and soil from a demolished thorium-extracting plant went into the sea in 1976.
In addition there had been three other instances of sea dumping off Scotland in the 1950s and 1960s.

Scrap from a radioactive valve manufacturing unit went into the Firth of Forth, two strontium-90 anti-static devices were disposed of off the island of Arran and material from the clear-up of a former radium factory went into the River Clyde.
In addition, 35,000 luminised dials containing radium were dumped either on land or into the North Sea in 1949, Rooker said.

"It is estimated that radioactive exposures to the public following any dispersal of radioactivity in the sea would give rise to radiation levels well within the International Commission on Radiological Protection recommended dose limit," he said in a written answer to a parliamentary question.

But he said despite this he was asking Britain's National Radiological Protection Board to assess the information unearthed by the ministry, which is part of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.
